https://www.dw.com/en/german-kidnapped-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IWgf A German citizen kidnapped in Niger was released to the Algerian military Image: Fateh Guidoum/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Algeria said on Saturday that a German citizen kidnapped by an armed criminal group some two weeks ago in neighboring Niger was safe and in the hands of the Algerian military. The German national was taken in charge by the Algerian army's security services on Friday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry shared on the official Algerian news agency. He has now been taken on a special flight from Guezzam in the far south to the Boufarik military base near the capital Algiers, it said, adding that he was in "good health" and would be handed to German authorities "at a later date." No details were provided on how the German national was freed. A spokesperson for the German Foreign Ministry told DW it was aware of the case, but added that the government "does not comment on cases involving the abduction of German citizens abroad." Niger, which has been under military rule since a July 2023 coup , has in the past few years been wracked by violence from jihadis linked to the al-Qaeda or the " Islamic State" (IS) terrorist groups. https://www.politico.eu/article/kaja-kal.text: The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Wednesday that the thwarted drone attack at Leipzig-Halle Airport bore “all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” after Germany blamed Russia for the incident. Speaking as the bloc’s foreign ministers gather in Wicklow, Ireland, Kallas said Germany’s attribution sent a “very strong signal” and praised EU governments for closing ranks behind Berlin. “We have already summoned the Russian ambassador, so have also many member states,” she said. “We will discuss what more can we do.” Advertisement Advertisement Other ministers struck an equally hard line. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called the attack part of a “long-running attempt by the Kremlin to destabilize the European Union, its democratic processes” and weaken support for Ukraine. “We will not let an act of such gravity go without consequences,” Barrot said, adding that France would support Germany’s sanctions proposals and propose measures against additional Russian vessels. Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said Europe had moved beyond talking simply about “hybrid threats.” “We’re talking about significant activity,” she said, accusing Moscow of a “very, very clear attempt” to divide EU governments and “put fear into citizens.” Berlin formally blamed Moscow on Tuesday for the Aug. 4 incident, in which three explosive-laden drones were detected around Leipzig-Halle Airport. Germany announced retaliatory diplomatic measures and plans to seek fresh EU sanctions. Russia denies any involvement. Kallas added that another 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex were already “in the pipeline.” No decision will be made at Wednesday’s meeting. But, she said, Germany has the political backing of its EU partners. “This is the unified response that we need.” Advertisement Advertisement

Europe Home page Europe 0 0 Romania misses out on last of EU pandemic recovery cash 30 August 2026 04:20 (UTC +04:00) Romania is set to lose around €770 million in EU recovery funds after its interim government and parliament failed to pass a key reform before a 31 August deadline, APA reports. The reform, part of Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), was intended to overhaul public-sector salaries and is tied to the country’s final recovery-fund milestones. Political disagreements prevented parliament from adopting it in time, the Romanian president’s office confirmed on Friday. The missed deadline means the funding is expected to be forfeited, even though the government had already factored the money into budgets and projects under way. The costs will now fall on Romania’s already stretched national finances. European Funds Minister Dragoș Pîslaru estimated that Romania would still absorb more than 90% of the grants available under the EU’s post-pandemic recovery fund.
